title: Burn-down and burn-up charts
blurb: Read burn-down and burn-up charts, spot slippage and scope change, and know what each chart is used for.
question: Six days into a ten-day iteration, the team's burn-down shows the actual line well above the ideal line. What does this mean, and what should the team focus on?

teach.h: Progress you can see at a glance
teach.body: Burn charts show progress, for example within a timebox or during an iteration, by plotting work completed and work still to do as lines that are updated regularly or daily. In PRINCE2 Agile, flexibility in what is delivered is the main performance aspect of interest, so a burn chart suits every level of the project. Tracking spend or time against tolerance adds little, because both have zero tolerance.

teach.caption: On day 6 the ideal is 16 points left but 27 remain. Above the ideal line means behind.

teach.body: A burn-down is a run chart of outstanding work over time. It is mostly used at team level, showing story points over the days of an iteration. The ideal line runs from the total at the start to zero at the end. Actual above ideal means not enough is being done: the team will not finish everything at this rate and should focus on the highest-priority items. Below the line means ahead; a rise means work was added.

teach.caption: The scope line steps up after iteration 4: work was added. The gap between the lines is the work still to do.

teach.body: A burn-up is a run chart of completed work against a deadline. It is often used at project or product level, showing story points over stages or iterations, to forecast likely completion dates. Because the total scope has its own line, any scope change is easy to see as that line moving. Slippage shows when the completed line, at its current slope, will not meet the scope line by the deadline.

rows.label: Behind when
values: Will not reach scope in time

teach.caption: An exception can be triggered by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level (Table 12.1).

teach.body: On day 6 of a ten-day iteration, the outpatient booking team's burn-down shows 27 points left against an ideal of 16. With the product owner, the team moves two Could-have stories back to the backlog and focuses on the Musts. At project level, project manager Gareth Lloyd's burn-up shows the scope line stepping from 100 to 120 points after the board approved a new clinic's epics, and the completed line suggests three more iterations.

teach.text: On a burn-DOWN, above the ideal line means BEHIND, not ahead. Do not confuse burn charts with the cumulative risk burn-down (total risk exposure across iterations, in the risk practice) or the cumulative flow diagram (tasks in each workflow state, revealing bottlenecks).

items: Burn charts show work done and work remaining, updated regularly or daily (12.4.3).
Burn-down: outstanding work over time; team level; days of an iteration.
Actual above ideal on a burn-down = behind; focus on the highest-priority items.
Burn-up: completed work against a deadline; project or product level; iterations or stages.
A rising scope line on a burn-up shows scope added.
Velocity = average story points delivered per timebox, used to forecast.

summary: You can now read burn-down and burn-up charts, tell when a team is behind or ahead, and spot scope change. You can also explain why burn charts suit every level of a PRINCE2 Agile project.

A.q: What does a burn-down chart show?
options: Completed work against a deadline
Tasks in each workflow state
Total risk exposure per iteration
Outstanding work over time
A.why: A burn-down is a run chart of outstanding work over time (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Completed work against a deadline is a burn-up chart.
whyNot.1: Tasks in each workflow state are shown by a cumulative flow diagram.
whyNot.2: Total risk exposure across iterations is a cumulative risk burn-down.

A.q: On an iteration burn-down chart, the actual line is above the ideal line. What does this mean?
options: The team is ahead and can pull in more stories
Scope has been cut since the iteration began
The team is behind the rate needed to finish
The team's velocity has risen this iteration
A.why: Actual above ideal means more work remains than planned: the team is behind and will not finish everything at this rate (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Being ahead would show the actual line below the ideal line.
whyNot.1: Cutting scope would pull the remaining line down, not leave it above the ideal.
whyNot.3: A rising velocity would bring the actual line down towards or below the ideal.

A.q: At which level is a burn-up chart MOST often used, and over what time axis?
options: Project or product level, over iterations or stages
Team level, over the days of an iteration
Board level, over the months of the budget year
Work package level, over hours of effort
A.why: A burn-up is often used at project or product level to show story points over stages or iterations and forecast completion (12.4.3).

whyNot.1: Team level over the days of an iteration describes a burn-down.
whyNot.2: Burn charts track what is delivered, not budget months.
whyNot.3: Burn charts plot story points, not hours of effort.

B.q: On a burn-up chart, the total scope line steps upwards after iteration 4. What does this show?
options: Work has been added to the scope
The team completed more stories
Some stories failed the DoD
The deadline has been moved later
B.why: On a burn-up the scope has its own line, so a step up means work was added to the total scope.

whyNot.1: Completed stories raise the completed-work line, not the scope line.
whyNot.2: Failing the DoD keeps stories off the completed line; it does not raise total scope.
whyNot.3: A later deadline moves the end point along the time axis; it does not lift the scope line.

B.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile see burn charts as natural at every level of a project?
options: They remove the need for exception reports
Flex in what is delivered is the key aspect
They show spend against the cost tolerance
They show each risk's probability and impact
B.why: Flexibility in what is delivered is the main performance aspect of interest, so showing it as a burn chart is natural at any level (12.3.1).

whyNot.0: Exception reports are still needed when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.
whyNot.2: Cost has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile, so tracking spend against tolerance adds little.
whyNot.3: Risk probability and impact are assessed in the risk practice, not shown by a burn chart.

B.q:
Which two statements about burn charts are correct?
1. A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline.
2. A burn-down chart shows the tasks in each workflow state.
3. Burn chart lines are updated regularly or daily.
4. Burn charts are used to track time tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: A burn-up shows completed work against a deadline (1), and burn chart lines are updated regularly or daily (3) (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 describes a cumulative flow diagram, not a burn-down.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: 2 is a cumulative flow diagram and 4 overlooks the zero tolerance on time.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: time has zero tolerance, so burn charts track what is delivered instead.

C.q: Halfway through an iteration, the burn-down shows the team cannot finish everything at its current rate. What should the team focus on?
options: Asking the board for an extra week
Adding a developer from another team
Starting the next iteration early
The highest-priority backlog items
C.why: With time fixed, a team that is behind focuses on the highest-priority items in the product backlog (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance; extending the iteration is not the PRINCE2 Agile response.
whyNot.1: Borrowing people from another team disrupts that team and does not address priority.
whyNot.2: The timebox is fixed; starting the next iteration early does not finish this one's priorities.

C.q: An updated burn chart forecasts that stage tolerances will be exceeded. What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest happens first?
options: Hold an immediate meeting to discuss options
Extend the stage end date by one iteration
Add the shortfall to the risk register
Wait for the next progress review workshop
C.why: Table 12.1: an exception can be triggered by an updated burn chart; hold an immediate meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board.

whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance; the project manager cannot extend the stage.
whyNot.2: A forecast breach of tolerance is an exception to act on now, not just a risk entry.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays the response; the guidance is to meet immediately.

C.q: Which chart shows how many tasks sit in each workflow state over time, helping a team find bottlenecks?
options: Burn-down chart
Burn-up chart
Cumulative flow diagram
Cumulative risk burn-down
C.why: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks (12.4.2).

whyNot.0: A burn-down shows outstanding work, not workflow states.
whyNot.1: A burn-up shows completed work against scope, not workflow states.
whyNot.3: A cumulative risk burn-down shows total risk exposure across iterations.

reteach.title: A tank draining and a jar filling
reteach.question: Picture a tank emptying and a jar filling. Which is the burn-down and which is the burn-up?

blocks.h: Two pictures of the same work
blocks.body: A burn-down is a tank draining: it starts full of work and should be empty at the end. If the level stays higher than planned, you are behind. A burn-up is a jar filling towards a line marked on the side: the line is the total scope. If someone raises the mark, the scope has grown, and you can see it at once.

blocks.text: Above the ideal line on a burn-down is bad news: more work is left than planned.

explain.body: A burn-down plots outstanding work over time. The ideal line runs from the total at the start of the iteration down to zero at the end.

test.q: On a burn-down chart, where does the ideal line start and end?
options: From zero up to the total
From the total down to zero
From the velocity to the deadline
From the first release to the last
test.why: The ideal line runs from the total work at the start down to zero at the end of the timebox.

whyNot.0: Rising from zero describes a completed-work line, as on a burn-up.
whyNot.2: Velocity is a rate, not a starting quantity of work.
whyNot.3: Releases are timeboxes on the release map, not the ends of the ideal line.

explain.body: Actual above ideal: behind, focus on the highest priorities. Actual below ideal: ahead of plan. A jump upwards: work has been added.

test.q: The actual line on an iteration burn-down is below the ideal line. What does this suggest?
options: The team is behind schedule
Scope has been added
The iteration has ended
The team is ahead of plan
test.why: Less work remains than the ideal line expects, so the team is ahead of plan.

whyNot.0: Behind schedule shows as the actual line above the ideal.
whyNot.1: Added scope shows as the remaining line jumping up.
whyNot.2: The end of the iteration is a point on the time axis, not the gap between lines.

explain.body: A burn-up plots completed work rising towards a separate total scope line, usually at project or product level over iterations or stages, so scope changes and the likely finish are easy to see.

test.q: Which chart makes scope change easiest to see?
options: Burn-down chart
Team skill matrix
Burn-up chart
Cumulative risk burn-down
test.why: A burn-up has a separate total scope line, so any change to scope shows as that line moving.

whyNot.0: On a burn-down, added scope is mixed into the remaining-work line and is harder to see.
whyNot.1: A team skill matrix shows skills and gaps, not scope.
whyNot.3: A cumulative risk burn-down shows risk exposure, not scope.

explain.body: Velocity, the average story points delivered per timebox, turns a burn chart into a forecast. If an updated burn chart forecasts tolerances being exceeded, hold an immediate meeting on options before escalating to the board.

options: average story points delivered per timebox
total story points left in the project backlog
number of iterations in a single release
hours a team works in each iteration
test.why: Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox for one or more teams (Glossary).

whyNot.1: Points left in the backlog are the remaining work, not a rate.
whyNot.2: Iterations per release describe the release map, not velocity.
whyNot.3: Velocity counts points delivered, not hours worked.
